newsitem.title: USA: Oldest astronaut hangs up space suit.
newsitem.headline: Oldest astronaut hangs up space suit.

text.p: Astronaut Story Musgrave, the oldest person to have been in orbit, has returned to Earth to stay after six space flights.

Musgrave and four fellow astronauts ended a nearly 18-day mission aboard shuttle Columbia with a touchdown in Florida Saturday. After nearly 30 years in the astronaut corps, NASA has decided to hang up Musgrave's space suit. Space agency officials have told him not to expect any more missions.
"I have had an incredible run of it," he said. "You also want to finish when you know that you're at your peak. I know that I'm probably peaked right here. I'm as good as I'm ever going to get."

Musgrave, 61, looks to be in great physical condition and is naturally exuberant. Appearing at a news conference several hours after landing, he was grinning from ear to ear and greeted some reporters with a bear hug.

The nametag "STORY" on his blue jump suit was upside down -- one of the shaven-headed Musgrave's trademark eccentricities. He is the oldest person to orbit the planet but he still has a youngster's sense of excitement and thirst for new experiences.

"The most exuberant child up there was Story Musgrave," Columbia's pilot Kent Rominger said, describing Musgrave as "the master of space" and adding: "Just seeing all this energy and the true love of flying in space from Story was very meaningful."
Musgrave says he hopes NASA can find some role for him in the future, perhaps as an "alternative thinker." He said he has squeezed every drop of enjoyment out of his six trips into space.

He records his experiences on index cards. While hundreds of NASA workers draft a detailed flight plan for each shuttle mission listing the precise times for satellite deployments, crew meals and communications link-ups, Musgrave compiles his own in a notebook.

One of the most enjoyable experiences, he said, was to black out the cockpit windows and turn off the lights. When the shuttle orbits into night, the window shades are opened and, with eyes accustomed to dark, an awesome sight awaits.

"To see all the heavens out there, the meteorites are coming in underneath; to see the city lights going by, the moon rising and to see the lightning ... It is a spiritual kind of thing to be floating in the window and to see that going by."
Columbia's mission was the longest shuttle flight ever and Musgrave described it as the perfect end for a space career.

"I just lived to the fullest in all the ways I could ... to try to accomplish the mission in the most perfect way I could and at the same time as a human being trying to experience in total what space flight really is," he said.
"This one was pure ecstasy. If this is the last space flight, this was the one to finish on."
